Conceptual Affinity. Certain bits of code want to be near other bits. They
have a certain conceptual affinity. The stronger that affinity, the less vertical
distance there should be between them.

As we have seen, this affinity might be based on a direct dependence, such
as one function calling another, or a function using a variable. But there are
other possible causes of affinity. Affinity might be caused because a group
of functions perform a similar operation. Consider this snippet of code from
Junit 4.3.1:



   public class Assert {
     static public void assertTrue(String message, boolean condition) {
       if (!condition)
         fail(message);
     }

     static public void assertTrue(boolean condition) {
       assertTrue(null, condition);
     }

     static public void assertFalse(String message, boolean condition) {
       assertTrue(message, !condition);
     }

     static public void assertFalse(boolean condition) {
       assertFalse(null, condition);
     }
   …

These functions have a strong conceptual affinity because they share a
common naming scheme and perform variations of the same basic task. The
fact that they call each other is secondary. Even if they didn’t, they would
still want to be close together.

Vertical Ordering

In general we want function call dependencies to point in the downward
direction. That is, a function that is called should be below a function that
does the calling.2 This creates a nice flow down the source code module
from high level to low level.
2. This is the exact opposite of languages like Pascal, C, and C++ that enforce functions to be
defined, or at least declared, before they are used.

As in newspaper articles, we expect the most important concepts to come
first, and we expect them to be expressed with the least amount of polluting
detail. We expect the low-level details to come last. This allows us to skim
source files, getting the gist from the first few functions, without having to
immerse ourselves in the details. Listing 5-5 is organized this way. Perhaps
even better examples are Listing 15-5 on page 263, and Listing 3-7 on page
50.



Horizontal Formatting

How wide should a line be? To answer that, let’s look at how wide lines are
in typical programs. Again, we examine the seven different projects. Figure
5-2 shows the distribution of line lengths of all seven projects. The
regularity is impressive, especially right around 45 characters. Indeed,
every size from 20 to 60 represents about 1 percent of the total number of
lines. That’s 40 percent! Perhaps another 30 percent are less than 10
characters wide. Remember this is a log scale, so the linear appearance of
the drop-off above 80 characters is really very significant. Programmers
clearly prefer short lines.

Figure 5-2 Java line width distribution

This suggests that we should strive to keep our lines short. The old
Hollerith limit of 80 is a bit arbitrary, and I’m not opposed to lines edging
out to 100 or even 120. But beyond that is probably just careless.

I used to follow the rule that you should never have to scroll to the right.
But monitors are too wide for that nowadays, and younger programmers
can shrink the font so small that they can get 200 characters across the
screen. Don’t do that. I personally set my limit at 120.



Horizontal Openness and Density

We use horizontal white space to associate things that are strongly related
and disassociate things that are more weakly related. Consider the following
function:
   private void measureLine(String line) {
     lineCount++;
     int lineSize = line.length();
     totalChars += lineSize;
     lineWidthHistogram.addLine(lineSize, lineCount);
     recordWidestLine(lineSize);
   }

I surrounded the assignment operators with white space to accentuate them.
Assignment statements have two distinct and major elements: the left side
and the right side. The spaces make that separation obvious.

On the other hand, I didn’t put spaces between the function names and the
opening parenthesis. This is because the function and its arguments are

[L19] 
[L20] When people look under the hood, we want them to be impressed with the
[L21] neatness, consistency, and attention to detail that they perceive. We want
[L22] them to be struck by the orderliness. We want their eyebrows to rise as they
[L23] scroll through the modules. We want them to perceive that professionals
[L24] have been at work. If instead they see a scrambled mass of code that looks
[L25] like it was written by a bevy of drunken sailors, then they are likely to
[L26] conclude that the same inattention to detail pervades every other aspect of
[L27] the project.
[L28] 
[L29] You should take care that your code is nicely formatted. You should choose
[L30] a set of simple rules that govern the format of your code, and then you
[L31] should consistently apply those rules. If you are working on a team, then the
[L32] team should agree to a single set of formatting rules and all members should
[L33] comply. It helps to have an automated tool that can apply those formatting
[L34] rules for you.
[L35] 
[L36] 
[L37] 
[L38] The Purpose of Formatting
[L39] 
[L40] First of all, let’s be clear. Code formatting is important. It is too important
[L41] to ignore and it is too important to treat religiously. Code formatting is
[L42] about communication, and communication is the professional developer’s
[L43] first order of business.
[L44] 
[L45] Perhaps you thought that “getting it working” was the first order of business
[L46] for a professional developer. I hope by now, however, that this book has
[L47] disabused you of that idea. The functionality that you create today has a
[L48] good chance of changing in the next release, but the readability of your
[L49] code will have a profound effect on all the changes that will ever be made.
[L50] The coding style and readability set precedents that continue to affect
[L51] maintainability and extensibility long after the original code has been
[L52] changed beyond recognition. Your style and discipline survives, even
[L53] though your code does not.

[L22] favorite formatting rules, but if he works in a team, then the team rules.
[L23] 
[L24] A team of developers should agree upon a single formatting style, and then
[L25] every member of that team should use that style. We want the software to
[L26] have a consistent style. We don’t want it to appear to have been written by a
[L27] bunch of disagreeing individuals.

[L30] to work out a coding style. This took about 10 minutes. We decided where
[L31] we’d put our braces, what our indent size would be, how we would name
[L32] classes, variables, and methods, and so forth. Then we encoded those rules
[L33] into the code formatter of our IDE and have stuck with them ever since.

[L36] FitNesse project.

[L1] This exposes the temporal coupling by creating a bucket brigade. Each
[L2] function produces a result that the next function needs, so there is no
[L3] reasonable way to call them out of order.
[L4] 
[L5] 
[L6] 
[L7] You might complain that this increases the complexity of the functions, and
[L8] you’d be right. But that extra syntactic complexity exposes the true
[L9] temporal complexity of the situation.
[L10] 
[L11] Note that I left the instance variables in place. I presume that they are
[L12] needed by private methods in the class. Even so, I want the arguments in
[L13] place to make the temporal coupling explicit.
[L14] 
[L15] G32: Don’t Be Arbitrary
[L16] 
[L17] Have a reason for the way you structure your code, and make sure that
[L18] reason is communicated by the structure of the code. If a structure appears
[L19] arbitrary, others will feel empowered to change it. If a structure appears
[L20] consistently throughout the system, others will use it and preserve the
[L21] convention. For example, I was recently merging changes to FitNesse and
[L22] discovered that one of our committers had done this:
[L23]    public class AliasLinkWidget extends ParentWidget
[L24]    {
[L25]      public static class VariableExpandingWidgetRoot {
[L26]        …
[L27] 
[L28]      …
[L29]    }
[L30] 
[L31] The problem with this was that VariableExpandingWidgetRoot had no need to be inside
[L32] the scope of AliasLinkWidget. Moreover, other unrelated classes made use of
[L33] AliasLinkWidget.VariableExpandingWidgetRoot. These classes had no need to know about
[L34] AliasLinkWidget.
[L35] 
[L36] Perhaps the programmer had plopped the VariableExpandingWidgetRoot into AliasWidget as
[L37] a matter of convenience, or perhaps he thought it really needed to be scoped
[L38] inside AliasWidget. Whatever the reason, the result wound up being arbitrary.
[L39] Public classes that are not utilities of some other class should not be scoped
[L40] inside another class. The convention is to make them public at the top level
[L41] of their package.
[L42] 
[L43] G33: Encapsulate Boundary Conditions
[L44] 
[L45] Boundary conditions are hard to keep track of. Put the processing for them
[L46] in one place. Don’t let them leak all over the code. We don’t want swarms
[L47] of +1s and -1s scattered hither and yon. Consider this simple example from
[L48] FIT:
[L49] 
[L50] 
[L51] 
[L52]    if(level + 1 < tags.length)
[L53]    {
[L54]      parts = new Parse(body, tags, level + 1, offset + endTag);
[L55]      body = null;
[L56]    }
[L57] 
[L58] Notice that level+1 appears twice. This is a boundary condition that should be
[L59] encapsulated within a variable named something like nextLevel.
[L60]    int nextLevel = level + 1;
[L61]    if(nextLevel < tags.length)
[L62]    {
[L63]      parts = new Parse(body, tags, nextLevel, offset + endTag);
[L64]      body = null;
[L65]    }
[L66] 
[L67] G34: Functions Should Descend Only One Level of Abstraction
[L68] 
[L69] The statements within a function should all be written at the same level of
[L70] abstraction, which should be one level below the operation described by the
[L71] name of the function. This may be the hardest of these heuristics to interpret
[L72] and follow. Though the idea is plain enough, humans are just far too good at
[L73] seamlessly mixing levels of abstraction. Consider, for example, the
[L74] following code taken from FitNesse:
[L75]    public String render() throws Exception
[L76]    {
[L77]      StringBuffer html = new StringBuffer(“<hr”);
[L78]      if(size > 0)
[L79]        html.append(” size=\“”).append(size + 1).append(”\“”);
[L80]      html.append(“>”);
[L81] 
[L82]      return html.toString();
[L83]    }
[L84] 
[L85] A moment’s study and you can see what’s going on. This function
[L86] constructs the HTML tag that draws a horizontal rule across the page. The
[L87] height of that rule is specified in the size variable.

According to “Clean Code” by Robert C. Martin, empirical measurements across seven large Java projects show that the vast majority of source‐code lines fall between 20 and 60 characters in length, with a pronounced peak around 45 characters and a sharp drop-off beyond 80 characters fileciteturn11file1L58-L64.  

From these observations, the author draws two practical guidelines:

1. **Strive for short lines.**  
   Programmers clearly prefer lines under 80 characters, and very few exceed 100.  

2. **Set a personal hard limit at 120 characters.**  
   While Martin is not ideologically opposed to lines up to 100 or even 120 characters — and acknowledges that modern widescreen monitors and font-shrinking can accommodate much longer lines — he cautions that anything beyond 120 characters is “probably just careless” fileciteturn11file1L70-L78.

In summary, aim to keep most lines well under 80 characters, but never exceed 120 characters to avoid horizontal scrolling and maintain optimal readability.

Use the **`SelectedValue`** property of your dropdown (not `"ValueMember"`) as the bound property, and point it at your DTO’s `AccountJson.RateTableGUID`. For example, assuming:

- `_accountDataBinding` is a `BindingSource` whose `DataSource` is your `ClientDto` (or wrapper thereof)  
- `AccountJson.RateTableGUID` is the `int` you want to read/write  

you would write:

```csharp
// after setting DataSource, DisplayMember, ValueMember:

// Clear any existing bindings:
guiRateTable.DataBindings.Clear();

// Bind the dropdown’s SelectedValue to your RateTableGUID property:
guiRateTable.DataBindings.Add(
    propertyName:  "SelectedValue",              // bind this control property
    dataSource:    _accountDataBinding,          // your BindingSource
    dataMember:    "AccountJson.RateTableGUID",  // CLR property path on the DTO
    formattingEnabled: true,
    dataSourceUpdateMode: DataSourceUpdateMode.OnPropertyChanged
);
```

**Explanation:**

1. **`DataSource`** / **`DisplayMember`** / **`ValueMember`**  
   You already have:
   ```csharp
   guiRateTable.DataSource    = rateTables;
   guiRateTable.DisplayMember = "TarriffTableName";
   guiRateTable.ValueMember   = "Id";
   ```
   which populates and configures the list.

2. **`SelectedValue`**  
   - The `SelectedValue` of the dropdown will be the `Id` of the chosen rate table.  
   - You bind that to your DTO’s `RateTableGUID` so that when the user changes the selection, the DTO is automatically updated.

3. **`BindingSource`**  
   - If you haven’t already, you need something like:
     ```csharp
     _accountDataBinding.DataSource = customerDto;
     ```
     so that `_accountDataBinding` knows about your `ClientDto`.

4. **`DataBindings.Add(...)`** signature  
   - **`propertyName`**: name of the control property (must be a public property—`"SelectedValue"` in this case).  
   - **`dataSource`**: usually a `BindingSource` or your DTO object.  
   - **`dataMember`**: the property (or dot-delimited path) on that data source.  
   - **`formattingEnabled`**: set to `true` if you want the binding engine to handle conversion/formatting.  
   - **`DataSourceUpdateMode.OnPropertyChanged`** makes sure changes flow back immediately when the selection changes.

With that in place, whenever the user picks a row in `guiRateTable`, your `customerDto.AccountJson.RateTableGUID` will be updated automatically—and if you change `AccountJson.RateTableGUID` in code, the dropdown will reflect that choice as well.

### **Cause of the Issue**

Your binding statement is likely similar to this:

```csharp

```

However, your `FuelSurCharge` property actually resides within the nested `AccountJson` object:

The binding engine **does not automatically traverse nested objects** unless explicitly instructed to do so.

---

### **Corrected Binding**

Specify the **full property path** within the binding, including the nested object (`AccountJson`):

```csharp
guiFuelSurCharge.DataBindings.Clear();
guiFuelSurCharge.DataBindings.Add(
    "Text", 
    _accountDataBinding, 
    "AccountJson.FuelSurCharge", 
    true, 
    DataSourceUpdateMode.OnPropertyChanged,

- **`"AccountJson.FuelSurCharge"`**: The complete and correct path to your nested property.
- **`DataSourceUpdateMode.OnPropertyChanged`**: Updates the data source immediately upon property change.
- **`"N0"`**: Numeric formatting with no decimal places (you can adjust formatting as needed).

_accountDataBinding.DataSource = customerDto;

The cause of the issue is that `nameof` does not provide the full property path—only the name of the last property in the path. Thus, this:

```

evaluates to just `"FuelSurCharge"`, **not** `"AccountJson.FuelSurCharge"`.

    "AccountJson.FuelSurCharge",
    true,

### Explanation:

- `nameof()` returns only the final property name.
- Nested properties in bindings must explicitly include the full object path.
- Thus, the correct binding must explicitly state `"AccountJson.FuelSurCharge"`.

## 1. Riemann Hypothesis (RH)

**Statement**  
All nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function  
\(\displaystyle \zeta(s)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty n^{-s}\)  
lie on the critical line \(\Re(s)=\tfrac12\) citeturn1search13.

**Equivalent Formulations**  
- **Primecounting error**:  
  \(\displaystyle \pi(x)=\operatorname{Li}(x)+O\bigl(x^{1/2}\ln x\bigr)\).  
- **Mertens bound**:  
  \(\displaystyle M(x)=\sum_{n\le x}\mu(n)=O\bigl(x^{1/2+\varepsilon}\bigr)\).  
- **HilbertPólya**: Existence of a selfadjoint operator whose eigenvalues correspond to the zeros.  
- **BeurlingNyman**: Closure of certain spaces in \(L^2(0,1)\).

**Evidence & Numerical Verification**  
- Over \(10^{13}\) zeros computed, all with \(\Re(s)=\tfrac12\).  
- Montgomerys paircorrelation matches GUE randommatrix statistics.  
- Zerofree regions proven off the line (classical zerodensity estimates).

**Implications**  
- **Sharper prime estimates**:  
  \(\pi(x)=\mathrm{Li}(x)+O(\sqrt{x}\ln x)\).  
- **Error control** in Chebyshev functions \(\psi(x)\), \(\vartheta(x)\).  
- Many equivalent conjectures in analytic number theory would follow.

## 2. Prime Number Theorem (PNT)

**Statement**  
\[
\pi(x)\sim\frac{x}{\ln x}\quad(x\to\infty),
\]  
equivalently the \(n\)th prime \(p_n\sim n\ln n\) citeturn4view0.

**Analytic Proof Outline**  
1. **Nonvanishing**: Hadamard & delaValléePoussin showed \(\zeta(s)\neq0\) on \(\Re(s)=1\).  
2. **Contour integration**:  
   \(\displaystyle \pi(x)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty}-\frac{\zeta'(s)}{\zeta(s)}\frac{x^s}{s}\,ds\),  
   shifting the line to \(\Re(s)=1+\varepsilon\) then to \(\Re(s)=\sigma<1\).

**Elementary Proof (SelbergErds)**  
- Avoids complex analysis via combinatorial identities (Selbergs symmetry formula).  
- Fully formalized in proof assistants (Isabelle/HOL, HOLLight).

**Numerical Data**  
- \(\pi(10^{14})=3\,204\,941\,750\,802\).  
- Relative error \(\bigl|\pi(x)-x/\ln x\bigr|/\pi(x)<10^{-3}\) for \(x<10^{14}\).

## 3. Twin Prime Conjecture

**Statement**  
There are infinitely many primes \(p\) with \(p+2\) also prime citeturn7view0.

**HardyLittlewood Heuristic**  
Define the **twinprime constant**  
\[
C_2=\prod_{p\ge3}\Bigl(1-\frac1{(p-1)^2}\Bigr)\approx0.6601618.
\]  
Then conjecturally  
\[
\pi_2(x)=\#\{p\le x:p+2\text{ prime}\}
\sim 2\,C_2\,\frac{x}{(\ln x)^2}.
\]

**Recent Progress**  
- **Yitang Zhang (2013)**: infinitely many prime pairs with gap \(7\times10^7\).  
- **MaynardTao**: improved to gap 246 (and, under ElliottHalberstam, down to 6).  
- **GPY method**: GoldstonPintzYldrms small gaps breakthrough.

**Rigorous Bounds**  
- **Bruns theorem**: \(\displaystyle \sum_{p,\;p+2\text{ prime}}\!\frac1p\) converges.  
- Upper bound:  
  \(\displaystyle \pi_2(x)=O\!\bigl(x/(\ln x)^2\bigr)\).

**Numerical Data**  
- **Twin primes below \(10^{18}\)**: 808675888577436 pairs.
